clips.text: Call 911 and get an AED. Start CPR immediately. Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface. Put the heel of one hand in the center of the chest and the other hand on top. Press hard and fast at 100–120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep, avoiding more than 2.4 inches. Allow full chest recoil. If trained, give 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. If unable or unwilling to give breaths, continue chest compressions. Turn on the AED as soon as available and follow its spoken instructions. Continue until professionals take over, normal breathing returns or you cannot continue safely. Important. For children or babies open the corresponding child or infant CPR guide. Rescue breaths are especially important for drowning-related and pediatric arrests.

clips.text: Call 911 using speakerphone if possible. Start CPR; ask someone to bring an AED. Lay the child face up on a hard, level surface. Place one or both hands on the lower half of the breastbone, depending on the child’s size. Give 30 compressions at 100–120 per minute, about 2 inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Let the chest fully rise between presses. If trained, open the airway with a gentle head tilt and chin lift, pinch the nose and give 2 breaths, each over about one second, enough for visible chest rise. Repeat 30:2. If unable to give breaths, keep compressing. Use an AED when available; follow its prompts. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or you cannot safely continue. Important. If alone without a phone, dispatcher activation timing depends on whether collapse was witnessed; if unwitnessed, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call and obtain an AED. Use infant CPR for a baby under 1.

clips.text: Call 911 and apply firm pressure immediately. Wear gloves or use a barrier if possible. Locate the source of bleeding. Press firmly and continuously with gauze or clean cloth. If an object is stuck in the wound, press around it, not on it. For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, apply a manufactured tourniquet if available and trained; follow dispatcher or device instructions. Keep the person warm and monitor breathing and responsiveness until help arrives. Important. Do not remove an embedded object; press around it. Do not loosen an applied tourniquet.

clips.text: For severe choking, call 911 or have someone call. If coughing forcefully, encourage coughing and watch closely. For severe choking in a conscious person age 1 or older, lean them forward and give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades. If still blocked, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts with your fist just above the navel and below the breastbone, pulling inward and upward. Use chest thrusts if pregnant or unable to encircle the abdomen. Repeat until the blockage clears or they become unresponsive. If unresponsive, lower safely, begin CPR and follow the dispatcher. Important. Never sweep the mouth blindly. Remove an object only if visible during CPR. Never use abdominal thrusts on babies.

clips.text: Call 911 using speakerphone if possible. Begin infant CPR; have someone get an AED. Place the infant face up on a firm, level surface. Use the heel of one hand or two thumbs with hands encircling the chest, pressing on the lower half of the breastbone. Give 30 compressions at 100–120 per minute, about 1½ inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Allow complete recoil. If trained, keep the head neutral, lift the chin, cover the infant’s mouth and nose with your mouth and give two gentle one-second breaths, just enough for chest rise. Repeat 30:2. If unable to give breaths, continue compressions. Apply an AED as soon as available; follow its prompts and use pediatric mode/pads if available. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or it is unsafe to continue. Important. Do not use adult compression depth. If alone without a phone after unwitnessed collapse, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call and obtain an AED. Not for resuscitation immediately after birth.

clips.text: For a person who will not wake up and is not breathing normally: call 911 and continue CPR while someone prepares the AED. Switch the device on and listen to its instructions. Expose the chest and wipe it dry. Apply pads to bare skin as shown on the device. For a small child or infant, prefer pediatric settings or pads when available; if pads could touch, use front-and-back placement as directed. Connect pads if required. Keep everyone clear while the device checks the heart rhythm. If the device advises a shock, ensure no one is touching the person; follow the shock instructions. Restart CPR immediately after a shock or a no-shock prompt. Follow the AED until professional help takes over. Important. Do not delay CPR to search for equipment. If pediatric pads are unavailable, use adult pads that do not touch. Do not touch the person during analysis or shock.

clips.text: Call 911 if this is a first seizure, it lasts 5 minutes or longer, repeats before recovery, occurs in water, causes injury, or breathing or recovery is impaired. Also call for a baby under 6 months, pregnancy, diabetes with unconsciousness, or if unsure. Note when the seizure starts. Stay nearby and clear dangerous objects away. Protect the head with something soft. Loosen tight clothing around the neck. If safe, gently turn the person onto their side; do not force movement. Important. Never restrain the person, put anything in their mouth or offer food or drink before they are fully alert. If uncertain, call 911.
